title: Reading and reasoning from graphs/tables
transcript: A graph connects each horizontal value to a vertical reading. Read the axis names and units before comparing points. A change is a difference between readings. A rate of change divides that difference by the distance along the horizontal axis.

In AMC Upper Primary questions, graphs and tables often represent the same information. Read the requested interval, row or category carefully. A Mawa style comparison can use a crossing point. At that point two rules give the same value, and their order may change afterwards.
The table shows cumulative counts at hours one to four: two, six, fourteen and twenty-one. How much did the count rise from hour two to hour four? The question asks for a change, not a final total.
The hour two count is six. The hour four count is twenty-one. Both readings use the same units. Subtract the earlier count from the later one. The increase is fifteen.

A chart shows times zero, two, five and nine minutes. The total counts at those times are zero, six, twenty-seven and forty-seven. During which interval was the rate of increase highest? The intervals have different lengths.

Divide each rise by its own time interval. The first rise is six over two minutes, giving three per minute. The next two rates are seven and five per minute. Use intervals of three minutes and four minutes. The highest rate is seven. This is the interval from minute two to minute five.

Plan A charges a fixed fee of fifteen dollars and then three dollars per visit. Plan B charges six dollars per visit with no fixed fee. At how many visits are the costs equal, and which plan is cheaper after that?

At a crossing the two costs are equal. A starts fifteen dollars higher, while B rises three dollars faster per visit. Divide to find the intersection at five visits. At that point both costs equal thirty dollars. After the crossing B is higher on the graph, because its cost rises faster. Plan A is cheaper beyond that visit count.
Test one visit after the crossover. A costs thirty-three dollars. B costs thirty-six dollars. B adds the larger amount every further visit, so the choice will not switch again.

Read both axis scales. A vertical rise alone doesn't tell you the rate if time intervals are different. At a crossing, both graph rules give the same value. Read the horizontal coordinate to find when it happens.

Label the horizontal and vertical quantities. Trace to the axis or row before performing a calculation. For a change, take a difference. For a rate, divide by the interval. For an intersection, check both rules at the same input.
